title: Dictionary-based named entity recognition
description: Dictionary NER finds archive entities by matching text against curated gazetteers of known names, the fastest reliable extraction baseline. Multi-word names load into a trie; the text is scanned left to right taking the longest match at each position, tagging spans with their entity type. It never invents entities, only recognizes listed ones. Use it to extract known people, places, and organizations from archive text.
demo:
gaz = {"justin addam higgins": "PERSON", "springfield": "PLACE"}
def longest_match(tokens, i):
    for L in range(3, 0, -1):
        phrase = " ".join(tokens[i:i+L]).lower()
        if phrase in gaz: return phrase, L
    return None, 0
tokens = "Justin Addam Higgins visited Springfield".split()
i, found = 0, []
while i < len(tokens):
    phrase, L = longest_match(tokens, i)
    if phrase: found.append((phrase, gaz[phrase])); i += L
    else: i += 1
print(found)
assert ("justin addam higgins", "PERSON") in found
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Pattern-based entity extraction rules
description: Pattern rules extract archive entities by textual shape — capitalized sequences, dates, measurements — without any dictionary. Regular expressions and orthographic rules (e.g., consecutive capitalized words form a candidate name) propose spans; stopword and context filters prune false positives. Rules catch novel entities dictionaries miss. Use it for entities too new or rare for any gazetteer.
demo:
import re
text = "Dr. Ada Lovelace met Alan Turing in 1952."
cands = re.findall(r"\b(?:[A-Z][a-z]+\s){1,2}[A-Z][a-z]+\b", text)
print("candidates:", cands)
assert "Ada Lovelace" in cands and "Alan Turing" in cands
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Frequency-based term extraction
description: Frequency extraction promotes repeated multi-word phrases to candidate entities using C-value style scoring. Candidate noun phrases are counted; a phrase's score discounts occurrences nested inside longer phrases, favoring the most informative level. Top scorers become the archive's emergent terminology. Use it to discover an archive's own vocabulary automatically.
demo:
from collections import Counter
import re
text = "archive intelligence guides archive intelligence systems"
words = text.split()
bigrams = [" ".join(words[i:i+2]) for i in range(len(words) - 1)]
scores = Counter(bigrams)
print(scores.most_common(1))
assert scores.most_common(1)[0][0] == "archive intelligence"
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Co-occurrence relation extraction
description: Co-occurrence extraction hypothesizes relations between entities that appear together unusually often in archive text. For entity pairs in the same sentence or window, pointwise mutual information separates meaningful co-occurrence from chance; high-PMI pairs become candidate edges. It is noisy but needs no training data. Use it to bootstrap a relation graph from raw archive text.
demo:
from collections import Counter
import math
sents = [["mars", "rover"], ["mars", "rover"], ["mars", "venus"], ["earth", "venus"]]
pair_c, single_c = Counter(), Counter()
for s in sents:
    for e in s: single_c[e] += 1
    for i in range(len(s)):
        for j in range(i+1, len(s)): pair_c[tuple(sorted((s[i], s[j])))] += 1
n = len(sents)
def pmi(a, b):
    p_ab = pair_c[tuple(sorted((a,b)))]/n
    return math.log(p_ab/((single_c[a]/n)*(single_c[b]/n)))
print("PMI(mars,rover) =", round(pmi("mars","rover"),2), "| PMI(mars,venus) =", round(pmi("mars","venus"),2))
assert pmi("mars","rover") > pmi("mars","venus")
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Hearst patterns for is-a relations
description: Hearst patterns extract taxonomic relations from lexico-syntactic templates like 'X such as Y' and 'Y and other X'. The builder scans for a small set of hand-written patterns; each match yields (hyponym, hypernym) pairs with the pattern as provenance. Precision is high, making them ideal seeds for taxonomy growth. Use it to grow clean is-a hierarchies from archive text.
demo:
import re
text = "Big predators such as lions and tigers."
m = re.search(r"(\w[\w ]*?) such as ([\w ]+?)\.", text)
hyper = m.group(1).strip()
hypos = [h.strip() for h in re.split(r",\s*|\s+and\s+", m.group(2))]
print(hyper, "<-", hypos)
assert hyper == "Big predators" and hypos == ["lions", "tigers"]

title: Dependency-pattern relation extraction
description: Dependency patterns extract relations from grammatical structure, catching relations that word order alone hides. Sentences parse into subject-verb-object triples via dependency arcs; the verb phrase becomes the predicate. It handles passive voice and long-distance relations that surface patterns miss. Use it for precise fact extraction from well-formed archive prose.
demo:
sent = [("Higgins", "nsubj"), ("built", "root"), ("archive", "dobj")]
subj = next(w for w, d in sent if d == "nsubj")
verb = next(w for w, d in sent if d == "root")
obj = next(w for w, d in sent if d == "dobj")
print((subj, verb, obj))
assert (subj, verb, obj) == ("Higgins", "built", "archive")

title: Subject-predicate-object triple store
description: A triple store holds the knowledge graph as (subject, predicate, object) facts with indexes on every permutation. Six indexes (spo, sop, pso, pos, osp, ops) or a pragmatic three make any triple pattern a fast lookup; the builder inserts extracted facts and answers pattern queries by joining bindings. It is the workhorse graph store. Use it as the core store of a built knowledge graph.
demo:
triples = [("mars", "is-a", "planet"), ("mars", "has", "rover"), ("venus", "is-a", "planet")]
def query(s=None, p=None, o=None):
    return [t for t in triples
            if (s is None or t[0]==s) and (p is None or t[1]==p) and (o is None or t[2]==o)]
print(query(p="is-a"))
assert len(query(p="is-a")) == 2
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Adjacency-dict property graph
description: An adjacency dict stores the graph as nested maps with properties on nodes and edges, ideal for in-memory graph building. Nodes map to attribute dicts and to neighbor maps keyed by edge with edge attributes; traversal is pointer-chasing with no index overhead. The builder uses it during construction before bulk-loading a store. Use it while constructing and validating the graph in memory.

title: Triple-pattern query matching
description: Triple-pattern matching answers graph queries by binding variables across patterns, the core of SPARQL-style querying. Each pattern (?x is-a planet) scans the matching index; bindings join across patterns on shared variables like a miniature database join. The builder uses it to validate and explore the constructed graph. Use it to query the built knowledge graph.

title: Blocking for entity resolution
description: Blocking groups candidate duplicate entities by cheap keys so pairwise comparison stays tractable at archive scale. Entities sharing a block key (e.g., year + name initial) are compared in detail; different blocks never compare, cutting O(n^2) to near-linear. Good blocking keeps recall high while slashing cost. Use it before pairwise entity matching on large archives.
demo:
from collections import defaultdict
ents = [("Higgins 2026", 1), ("Higgins 2025", 2), ("Lovelace 1843", 3)]
blocks = defaultdict(list)
for e, i in ents:
    blocks[e.split()[0][0] + e.split()[-1]].append(i)
print(dict(blocks))
assert blocks["H2026"] == [1]
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Pairwise entity comparison and merging
description: Pairwise comparison scores candidate entity pairs on field similarities and merges those above threshold. Name similarity (Jaro-Winkler or token overlap), date closeness, and shared attributes combine into a match score; pairs above threshold merge into canonical entities with merged provenance. It dedupes the graph's nodes. Use it to collapse duplicate entities from multiple archive sources.
demo:
def jacc(a, b):
    sa, sb = set(a.lower().split()), set(b.lower().split())
    return len(sa & sb)/len(sa | sb)
pairs = [("Mars Rover", "mars rover"), ("Mars Rover", "Venus Orbiter")]
merged = [p for p in pairs if jacc(*p) > 0.8]
print("merged:", merged)
assert merged == [("Mars Rover", "mars rover")]
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Canonical entity merging with provenance
description: Canonical merging fuses matched entities into one node that remembers every source it came from. The survivor keeps the richest attributes; all variant names become aliases and each carries its source ID. Future extractions match against aliases, so the graph converges instead of re-splitting. Use it to keep the built graph's entities clean as new archives arrive.

title: Schema constraint checking on graphs
description: Constraint checking validates the built graph against shape rules, catching extraction errors before they pollute the archive. Shapes declare required properties and value types per node class (e.g., every planet needs exactly one orbital-period number); the validator reports violations with the offending nodes. It is SHACL-style validation in miniature. Use it as the quality gate on graph construction.

title: Orphan node detection in built graphs
description: Orphan detection finds graph nodes with no edges, usually extraction failures or isolated facts worth review. The validator scans adjacency for nodes with zero in- and out-degree and reports them with their source sentences; reviewers confirm, connect, or delete them. It keeps the graph navigable. Use it to keep the built knowledge graph connected and useful.

title: Provenance stamping on graph facts
description: Provenance stamping records the source and extraction method of every graph fact so the graph stays auditable. Each triple carries source document ID, extractor name, and confidence; queries can filter by provenance and retractions delete by source. Trust in the graph becomes traceable. Use it so every built fact can be traced to its archive source.
demo:
facts = []
def stamp(s, p, o, src, conf):
    facts.append({"s": s, "p": p, "o": o, "src": src, "conf": conf})
stamp("mars", "is-a", "planet", "doc-7", 0.95)
trusted = [f for f in facts if f["conf"] >= 0.9]
print("trusted facts:", len(trusted))
assert len(trusted) == 1 and trusted[0]["src"] == "doc-7"
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice
